definition: A contextual derivative statement must identify the input, output, instant, units, and practical meaning. Positive and negative values describe direction of change, not whether the quantity itself is positive.
Linearization uses the tangent line as a nearby approximation. Accuracy improves near the center point and depends on curvature and input distance.
Position, velocity, and acceleration are successive layers of change. Their signs and zeros describe direction, speed changes, turning, and concavity, while their units distinguish the quantities.

Related-rates problems connect quantities that change together. An equation describes the geometric or physical relationship; differentiating with respect to time turns that relation into a rate equation.
